entry.evidence: However, it is still challenging to define the scale of a TIH, because even if a dense network of global navigation satellite system (GNSS) receivers [...]

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), with PDF for figure pages

steps.action: The authors take from earlier work the physical mechanism of tsunami ionospheric hole (TIH) formation: tsunami-generated acoustic waves move plasma downward, which causes recombination and a drop in TEC.
steps.quote: The downward plasma causes recombination, and ion production is suppressed, resulting in a decrease in TEC

steps.action: The authors take from Kamogawa et al. (2016) the positive correlation between initial-tsunami height and the rate of TEC depression across tsunami cases.
steps.quote: They discovered a positive correlation between the initial-tsunami height and the rate of TEC depression.

steps.action: The authors pose the problem of defining the scale of a TIH from sparse, moving, non-uniform TEC measurement points.
steps.quote: it is still challenging to define the scale of a TIH

steps.action: The authors propose a statistical surface-fitting method that estimates TEC where there are no measurements and uses the hole volume, with uncertainty, as the TIH measure.
steps.quote: we propose to use its volume as a measure of the TIH

steps.action: The authors check the 300 km thin-shell ionosphere assumption against the Kokubunji ionogram peak height (306 km) reported for the event day.
steps.quote: This result suggests that the assumption of a hypothetical thin ionosphere at an altitude of 300 km in our analysis is reasonable.

steps.action: The authors derive slant TEC from dual-frequency GEONET phase delays, remove a quadratic pre-event baseline, project to vertical, and apply a 300 s backward moving average to keep the depression signal.
steps.quote: TEC between the GNSS satellites and the GNSS receivers can be estimated from the phase delay of these two types of radio signals

steps.action: The authors build the pipeline: k-nearest-neighbour outlier removal, then Gaussian process regression with a Matérn (ν=5/2) kernel plus nugget, accelerated with INLA-SPDE on a finite-element mesh of about 5200 elements.
steps.quote: We employ here the Matérn kernel with an additional nugget that accounts for some noise about the observations

steps.action: The authors benchmark computational time for INLA-SPDE against standard GP regression (43.1 s versus 763.9 s mean).
steps.quote: whereas the average computational time based on the standard GP regression method is more than 10 min

steps.action: The authors display measured TEC at four times and show that the measurement points move, are non-uniform, and that a single minimum value cannot capture TIH width or anisotropy.
steps.quote: the measurement points are moving and are not uniformly distributed in the targeting range

steps.action: The authors validate the two detected outliers with a 3D plot, a semi-variogram cloud, and GSI records showing that those receivers or antennas were later replaced; the outliers are removed from all analyses.
steps.quote: to validate further, we create a semi-variogram cloud

steps.action: The authors fit the TEC surface with uncertainty to the full data at 06:08:30 and estimate TEC on a 0.01° grid, capturing an anisotropic TIH offset from the epicentre.
steps.quote: The fitted surface in Fig. c is an almost perfect fit to the TEC data observed by the satellites.

steps.action: The authors compare the fitted TIH shape and region with the initial tsunami from the T. Saito et al. (2011) inversion and find them almost the same.
steps.quote: the shape and region of the TIH region are almost the same as those of the initial tsunami shown by the simulation

steps.action: The authors refit using random 5% subsets of receivers (40 receivers, 10 random draws); they compare minimum values, TIH maps and TIH volumes with the full-data case and compute the probability that a draw misses the TIH.
steps.quote: 10 experiments were conducted to randomly select 5 % of receivers

steps.action: The authors map TIH expansion at the −2, −3 and −4 TECU thresholds and track the maximum expansion distance in eight directions from the tsunami source over time.
steps.quote: the expansion of the TIH in the eastern and southwestern directions is more pronounced than in the other directions

steps.action: The authors overlay the −3 and −4 TECU TIH regions on the T. Saito et al. (2011) initial-tsunami inversion and find that they mostly overlap.
steps.quote: the initial tsunami estimated by using inversion analysis mostly overlaps with the TIH where the TEC reduction is large

steps.action: Using the uncertainty map, the authors reject larger estimation uncertainty as the cause of the TIH extending east of the initial-tsunami area.
steps.quote: it is unlikely that this was the reason for capturing the non-overlapping phenomenon

steps.action: The authors propose that the eastward extension arises because the initial-tsunami height peaks on the Japan Trench and acoustic effects spread evenly east and west from there.
steps.quote: the initial-tsunami height is highest on the Japan Trench

steps.action: The authors check the TIH overlap against two further independent initial-tsunami estimates (Ohta et al. 2012; Takagawa and Tomita 2012), digitised by eye.
steps.quote: where these initial tsunamis are roughly estimated by looking at them

steps.action: The authors compare TEC depth profiles with initial-tsunami height along the latitude and longitude of maximum height, and as time series, using data supplied by T. Saito.
steps.quote: the longitude with the largest decrease in TEC and the longitude with the highest initial-tsunami height roughly match

steps.action: The authors compute the TIH volume time series, with one-sided 80% and 99% CIs, by trapezoidal quadrature over the negative-TEC region of the fitted surface, for full and sparse data.
steps.quote: computed by the trapezoidal quadrature method for the region where TEC estimated by surface fitting has a negative value

steps.action: The authors compute the volume with both standard GP regression and INLA-SPDE, and average the sparse-data volumes over 10 random selections to remove seed effects.
steps.quote: In Fig. a, surface fitting is implemented with simple GP regression, while the INLA-SPDE method is applied to the GP regression process in Fig. b.

steps.action: The authors set a provisional warning threshold of 200 000 TECU km² (about 10–20% of the maximum TIH volume), reasoning from the depression ratios in Kamogawa et al. (2016).
steps.quote: a provisional threshold is set to 200 000 TECU km 2

steps.action: The authors compare threshold-crossing times for the fitted surface and its 80% and 99% CIs, for full and sparse data, and find a warning within 15 min with only 1–4 min of delay due to uncertainty.
steps.quote: delays for advisories of only, respectively, 1–2 or 2–4 min

steps.action: Because the INLA-SPDE meshing sometimes fails for sparse data, the authors fall back on standard GP regression, which runs in under 10 s for the sparse case.
steps.quote: our implementation of the INLA-SPDE method sometimes fails due to the geometric meshing optimized for larger data sets

steps.action: The authors compare the smaller northward than southward expansion with Heki and Ping (2005) and with 3D simulations (Zettergren et al.), and contrast it with the 2D simulation of Shinagawa et al. (2013).
steps.quote: it is confirmed that the northward expansion is smaller than the southward expansion, no matter at which threshold level

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that the method computes TIH volume in real time with uncertainty, robust to sparse non-uniform data, and usable for warnings.
steps.quote: we compute the volume of the ionospheric depression generated by a tsunami, in real time and with enough confidence to issue warnings

tree.answer: TIH after the 2011 Tohoku-Oki tsunami, established in prior work
No; TEC is sampled at sparse moving points, so the full hole must be inferred
Estimate TIH volume with uncertainty in real time for tsunami warning
No formal rivals; the single-minimum-value metric is set aside, and an uncertainty artifact is rejected for the eastward extension
Conditions found: one live event (Tohoku-Oki 2011) in the archived GEONET data

tree.answer: Not yet; one event only, other tsunamis deferred to future work
Yes; 5% random receiver subsets, GP versus INLA-SPDE, and repeated draws
Kept: method characterised; warning threshold crossed within 15 min

end.claim: Gaussian process surface fitting (GP or INLA-SPDE) computes the volume of the tsunami ionospheric hole with uncertainty in real time, even from 5% of GEONET receivers, and crosses a provisional warning threshold within 15 min of the 2011 Tohoku-Oki earthquake.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the GP regression with Matérn kernel and INLA-SPDE, which interpolates TEC with uncertainty over unmeasured areas, there would be no TIH volume or confidence interval to threshold.

gates.evidence: The data are archived GEONET observations of one event, not acquired under a hypothesis. The sparse-data test could have failed: volumes from 5% subsets could have diverged from the full-data volumes (§3.3 ¶8). The overlap with the initial tsunami is judged visually, without a metric (§3.6 ¶5: 'roughly estimated by looking at them'). The 200 000 TECU km² threshold was set as 10–20% of the maximum TIH volume of this same event (§3.8 ¶4), so it was fixed after the data were seen.

SPDE approach with integrated nested Laplace approximation and Gauss–Markov random fields (Lindgren et al. 2011; Rue et al. 2009)
k-nearest neighbour algorithm for outlier detection (Cover and Hart 1967)

novelty_claims.quote: We develop a new method to analyze the total electron content (TEC) depression in the ionosphere after a tsunami occurrence.
We show here for the first time that our method of estimating the entire TIH by GP regression can be used to estimate the initial-tsunami [...]
Our method is the first to demonstrate that we can calculate the volume of TIHs accurately in real time
we have confirmed for the first time that the westward expansion of the TIH with TEC less than - 3
shows for the first time that the TIH reflects the shape of the initial tsunami at that fixed latitude and longitude

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: (1) The TIH overlaps the initial-tsunami region (best_explanation): the comparison is visual, and two of the three references were digitised by eye; no overlap metric is reported. (2) Directional expansion and asymmetry of the TIH (estimate without stated resolution): uncertainty is not propagated into the expansion distances. (3) A warning within 15 min (provisional): the threshold is derived from this same event's maximum volume and is not validated on other events. Only one tsunami is analysed; generalization is asserted ('very likely ... around the world') but not tested. The relation between volume and tsunami size is deferred to future work. Several processing choices are not varied: the 300 km shell height, the 300 s filter, the quadratic baseline window, the kNN k and the Matérn ν. Inference: the full-data surface is treated as the reference truth for the sparse tests, so the sparse test checks consistency, not accuracy. No supplement content or review file was coded. The paper reports two anonymous referees, but no review sequence could be coded.

disagreements.target: Kamogawa et al. (2016), minimum observed TEC value as the scale of a TIH
disagreements.support: Table 2 shows the minimum value varying across random receiver subsets while the TIH volume stays stable; the fitted surfaces show width and anisotropy that a single value cannot capture.
disagreements.quote: using one specific data point such as the minimum observed value as a scale of a TIH is insufficient to characterize the initial wave

disagreements.target: Previous papers based on unfiltered observation data reporting that the TIH stops above the tsunami source
disagreements.support: Threshold-based expansion maps and distance time series show that the −2 TECU region expands over time.
disagreements.quote: a more detailed analysis in our study shows that the TIH with a threshold of TEC variation below - 2 expands over time

disagreements.target: Liu et al. (2019, 2020), TEC-based tsunami source estimation
disagreements.support: The GP surface covers the whole target area, so it estimates a source region rather than a point.
disagreements.quote: these studies estimate the tsunami source [...]

disagreements.target: Shinagawa et al. (2013), 2D simulation of the TIH
disagreements.support: The observed larger southward than northward TEC decrease agrees with the 3D simulations (Zettergren et al.) rather than the 2D one.
disagreements.quote: While the results of the 2D simulations did not show a relatively large decrease in TEC to the south

disagreements.target: Heki and Ping (2005), expectation of an even east–west spread
disagreements.support: The TIH extends east of the initial-tsunami area; this is attributed to the height maximum on the Japan Trench, after an uncertainty artifact is ruled out.
disagreements.quote: According to this principle, the TIH is expected to spread evenly in the east–west direction of the tsunami generation area.

disagreements.target: Seismology-based initial-tsunami estimation for warnings (community practice)
disagreements.support: Cites the underestimated Mw 7.9 initial value for Tohoku, tsunami earthquakes, and gap–slip mismatches as motivation for a seismology-independent measure.
disagreements.quote: the initial-tsunami wave cannot be precisely inferred from seismic information alone
